title: Decisiveness of static probabilistic Petri nets for finite targets
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides the following problem? The input is a finite Petri net with positive constant integer transition weights, an initial marking \(m_0\), and a finite explicitly listed set \(A\) of target markings. In the induced discrete-time Markov chain, let \(U_A\) consist of markings from which no marking in \(A\) is reachable by a finite sequence of enabled transitions. Decide whether \[\Pr_{m_0}\bigl[\exists n\in\mathbb N:\ M_n\in A\cup U_A\bigr]=1.\] This property is decisiveness from \(m_0\) with respect to \(A\). We retain the source's static-weight, finite-target question; its other, dynamic-weight variant is already resolved negatively and is described in the context.

source_formulation.text: For probabilistic Petri nets with constant transition weights, is decisiveness with respect to a supplied initial marking and a finite target set decidable?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source’s remaining static-weight question

why: Decisiveness says that unresolved probability mass almost surely disappears: a run eventually either succeeds or enters a state from which success is impossible. This supports certified approximation of reachability probabilities in infinite-state systems. Deciding the property for ordinary constant-weight Petri nets would identify exactly when this general verification guarantee can be recognized from a finite concurrent-system description.
status_note: The retained static-weight finite-target question is explicit in CONCUR 2023 and in the 2025 follow-up author presentation. The QEST+FORMATS 2025 paper’s conclusion retains constant-weight Petri nets; its undecidability theorem permits affine marking-dependent weights. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution for the defined static class. This source-open assessment does not independently certify all cited proofs or exhaust later literature.

progress.text: The 2023 source cites the decisive-Markov-chain theorem implying decisiveness of static probabilistic Petri nets for upward-closed targets.
The source explicitly leaves static finite-target recognition open while proving undecidability for polynomial dynamic weights and decisiveness for its regular-language subclass.
The follow-up proves undecidability already with affine marking-dependent weights and retains the constant-weight case in its concluding research questions.

importance.reason: A precise unresolved recognition boundary for a foundational probabilistic concurrency model. Static upward-closed targets and dynamic-weight undecidability leave a meaningful finite-target gap whose resolution would clarify the applicability of general reachability-probability approximation guarantees.

sentences: A static probabilistic Petri net randomly chooses an enabled transition according to its fixed positive weight.
Decisiveness for a finite target means that almost every run eventually reaches either the target or a marking from which the target is unreachable.
The question asks whether this property is decidable from the net, one initial marking and an explicit finite target set.
Known upward-closed-target guarantees and undecidability with marking-dependent weights do not settle this constant-weight finite-target case.
A resolution would clarify when a general guarantee supporting certified probability approximation can be recognized in an ordinary probabilistic counter model.

definitions: Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). The net consists of a finite set of places \(P\), a finite set of transitions \(T\), input and output vectors \(\mathrm{Pre}(t),\mathrm{Post}(t)\in\mathbb N^P\), and weights \(w(t)\in\mathbb N\setminus\{0\}\). A marking \(m\in\mathbb N^P\) records the number of tokens in each place. Transition \(t\) is enabled exactly when \(m\ge\mathrm{Pre}(t)\) componentwise; firing it gives \(m-\mathrm{Pre}(t)+\mathrm{Post}(t)\). There are no inhibitor, reset or transfer arcs and no extra zero tests. Write \(E(m)\) for the set of enabled transitions. If it is nonempty, select each \(t\in E(m)\) with probability \(w(t)/\sum_{r\in E(m)}w(r)\), and fire it once. If several transitions yield the same successor, their probabilities add. Each listed transition receives its one weight regardless of how many token subsets could enable it. If \(E(m)\) is empty, the chain stays at \(m\) with probability one. The weight of a transition never changes with the marking. All weights, token counts and finite incidence tables are explicitly encoded in binary; the numbers of places, transitions and target markings are unrestricted. The chain \((M_n)_{n\ge0}\) starts at \(M_0=m_0\) and uses the probability measure on infinite paths whose finite-prefix probabilities are the products of the corresponding transition probabilities. Reachability is reflexive, so a target is reached at time zero and \(A\cap U_A=\varnothing\). The empty target set is allowed and makes \(U_A\) the entire state space. The machine must make the exact yes/no decision on every finite input, with no oracle, random error, time limit or probability tolerance. The initial marking is part of the input; the question does not quantify over all initial markings at once.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability for precisely these constant-weight nets, supplied initial markings and arbitrary finite targets. A positive answer must specify one uniform total computable algorithm and prove its equivalence with the displayed probability-one predicate. A negative answer must prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. Nondecisiveness of some example is not an undecidability proof. A result for weights depending on the current marking, or for targets given only as upward-closed sets, does not settle the retained static finite-target problem.

context_blocks.text: Decisiveness does not require reaching the target with probability one. It also permits reaching the avoid set, where the target is no longer reachable at all. The obstruction is positive probability of continuing forever outside the target while retaining some finite path to it at every visited state.

Constant transition weights still produce state-dependent probabilities: which transitions are enabled changes with the current marking. The model makes this dependence only through enabling and normalization. Assigning a weight that grows with a token count is a different, dynamic model.

A one-place net illustrates why static weights do not automatically ensure finite-target decisiveness. Give the increment transition weight two and the decrement transition weight one, with decrement enabled only above zero. Starting at one and targeting zero gives an upward-biased random walk: zero remains reachable everywhere, yet the probability of never hitting it is positive. This defeats decisiveness, while a universal recognition algorithm could still in principle classify the instance.

For constant-weight nets, upward-closed targets are known to be decisive. An upward-closed set contains every marking obtained by adding tokens to one of its elements. A finite exact target set generally lacks this closure, so the established theorem does not apply to the question here.

The same 2023 source resolves its dynamic-weight question: polynomial marking-dependent weights make decisiveness undecidable even for finite or upward-closed targets. Its Theorem 22 also identifies a positive subclass with a regular firing language. The active question retained here is the separately stated constant-weight finite-target case; the resolved dynamic variant is not presented as still open.

The 2025 paper strengthens the dynamic-weight negative theorem to affine functions of one place marking. Its conclusion and the authors’ presentation retain static Petri nets with finite targets as a further question. Dependence on even one place remains genuine dependence, so the improved negative theorem does not reach the constant-weight class.
